Counterexamples to a conjecture and improved bounds for bipanchromatic colorings

We study the bipanchromatic number \(\chi_B\), introduced by Lalou et al. [1] as the maximum number of colors in a panchromatic hypergraph coloring where every color appears at least twice. They show that merging uniquely occurring colors in a maximum panchromatic coloring gives the lower bound \(\beta=\chi_P-\lceil\alpha/2\rceil\le\chi_B\), where \(\chi_P\) is the panchromatic number and \(\alpha\) is the minimum number of such colors among maximum panchromatic colorings. They conjectured that \(\chi_B=\beta\) and subsequently disproved it [5]. We identify the smallest counterexample, with six vertices and three hyperedges, both minimum possible. We show that the ratio bound \(\chi_B/\beta<2\) is asymptotically sharp and prove minimality results for the order and hyperedge count. For \(3\le\alpha<\chi_P\) we show that every integer from \(\beta\) to \(\chi_P-1\) occurs as \(\chi_B\) while \(\chi_P\) and \(\alpha\) are held fixed. Furthermore, we discover that the values \(|V|,\chi_P,\alpha\) directly decide whether the conjectured equality holds except when \(\alpha=4\), where a matching reduction resolves the ambiguity. We derive the optimal universal lower bound _L_ depending only on \(|V|,\chi_P,\alpha\) in the nontrivial regime \(0<2\alpha<|V|\). Finally, we prove \(\chi_B/L\le 5/4\) and \(\chi_B/L\le 6/5+1/(5L)\), with 5/4 sharp and 6/5 asymptotically sharp as \(L\rightarrow\infty\).

## 1 Introduction

A _panchromatic_ coloring [1, 2, 3, 4] uses every color in every hyperedge, with maximum \(\chi_P\) colors. Lalou et al. [1] introduced bipanchromatic colorings to study completely independent spanning trees in split graphs. These colorings use each color at least twice overall, with maximum \(\chi_B\). Let \(\alpha\) be the minimum number of colors occurring once in a \(\chi_P\)-coloring. Their conjecture [1, Conjecture 1] predicts \(\chi_B=\chi_P-\lceil\alpha/2\rceil\) by merging those colors.

The same authors subsequently disproved this conjecture [5]. They construct counterexamples as three-hyperedge sunflowers with a common set of 6_d_ vertices and three disjoint petals of size _q_, where \(d\ge 1\) and \(q\ge 2d\). Their parameters are \(\chi_P=6d+q\), \(\alpha=6d\), and \(\chi_B=4d+q\). Thus the conjectured value is exceeded by exactly _d_, on \(6d+3q\ge 12d\) vertices.

Our three-hyperedge construction uses 12_d_-6 vertices for the same excess (Proposition 2). Without restricting the number of hyperedges, we prove that the minimum order is 4_d_+2 and classify all examples attaining it (Theorem 6). Their family has actual-to-conjectured ratio at most \(\frac{6}{5}\). We determine the sharp worst-case ratio over all hypergraphs, proving that it is strictly below two and can approach two (Theorem 5). We develop the coloring bounds and equality criteria suggested in their concluding remarks [5, Section 5].

Sections 2-3 introduce the colorings and counterexamples. Section 4 establishes sharp bounds and characterizes minimum-size counterexamples. Section 5 determines, with minimum order, all possible \(\chi_B\) values with fixed \(\chi_P\) and \(\alpha\), showing that no formula depending only on \(\chi_P\) and \(\alpha\) can determine \(\chi_B\) for every hypergraph. Section 6 shows that the hypergraph order, \(\chi_P\) and \(\alpha\) determine if the conjectured equality holds, except when \(\alpha=4\) which is resolved by maximum matching. In Section 7, the optimal lower bound _L_ for \(\chi_B\) is determined from |_V_|, \(\chi_P\) and \(\alpha\), with \(\chi_B/L\le 5/4\) and \(\chi_B/L\le 6/5+1/(5L)\), where 5/4 is sharp and 6/5 is asymptotically sharp as \(L\rightarrow\infty\).

## 2 Preliminaries

A hypergraph _H_=(_V,_E) consists of a non-empty set _V=V(H_) (the vertices of _H_) and a hyperedge set \(E(H)=\mathcal{E}\subset\mathcal{P}(V)\). If every hyperedge of _H_ contains exactly _r_ vertices, _H_ is _r_-uniform. A proper coloring of a hypergraph assigns colors to its vertices so that no hyperedge of size at least two is monochromatic.

**Definition 1** (Panchromatic colors)**.** A _panchromatic k-coloring_ of _H_ assigns _k_ colors to its vertices so that each hyperedge contains at least one vertex of each color. The maximum such _k_ is the _panchromatic number_ \(\chi_P(H)\).

**Definition 2** (Minimum unique-color count)**.** A color is _unique_ in a panchromatic coloring of _H_ if it is used on exactly one vertex. For every integer \(k\in[\chi_P(H)]\), let \(\alpha_k(H)\) denote the minimum number of vertices with unique colors among all panchromatic _k_-colorings of _H_. By convention, \(\alpha_0(H)=0\).

**Definition 3** (Bipanchromatic colors)**.** A panchromatic _k_-coloring is _bipanchromatic_ \[1\] if no color is unique. The _bipanchromatic number_ \(\chi_B(H)\) of _H_ is the maximum _k_ such that _H_ admits a bipanchromatic coloring. <sup>1</sup>

Observe that \(\chi_B(H)=max\{k\in\mathbb{N}:\alpha_k=0\}\). Since every color appears on at least two vertices, it follows that \(\chi_B(H)\le\lfloor|V|/2\rfloor\).

When the hypergraph _H_ is implied, we omit the argument _H_ and write \(\chi_P\), \(\chi_B\), and \(\alpha_k\). Write \(\alpha=\alpha_{\chi_P}\). Lalou et al. \[1, Conjecture 1\] conjectured that

\(\chi_B=\chi_P-\left\lceil\frac{\alpha}{2}\right\rceil.\) (1)

This equality was disproved in \[5, Proposition 1\]. For \(|V|\ge 2\), choose a panchromatic \(\chi_P\)- coloring with \(\alpha\) unique colors. Merge the unique colors in pairs. If one unique color remains, merge it with any other color. This results in a bipanchromatic coloring with \(\chi_P-\lceil\alpha/2\rceil\) colors. Thus, \(\chi_P-\lceil\alpha/2\rceil\) is a lower bound for \(\chi_B\). The equality in \[1, Conjecture 1\] would mean that this merging procedure is optimal. The examples in Section 3 have bipanchromatic colorings with more colors than this procedure produces. We define _excess_ \(\epsilon=\chi_B-(\chi_P-\lceil\alpha/2\rceil)\) which measures the difference between \(\chi_B\) and the lower bound in (1).

## 3 Counterexamples

The _sunflower_ S_<sub>n</sub>_=(_V,_E) is an (_n_+1)-uniform hypergraph with 2_n_ vertices and _n_ hyperedges. The set of vertices is \(V=S\sqcup P\), where _S_={_s_<sub>1</sub>_,...,s<sub>n</sub>_} and _P_={_p_<sub>1</sub>_,...,p<sub>n</sub>_} are disjoint, and its hyperedges are \(e_i=S\cup\{p_i\}\) for all \(i\in[n]\).

**Theorem 1** (Sunflower counterexamples)**.** _For_ S_<sub>n</sub> with_ \(n\ge 3\),

\(\chi_P=n+1,\alpha=n,\chi_B=n.\) (2)

_Consequently,_ \(\epsilon=\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil-1\ge 1\)_, so every_ S_<sub>n</sub> is a counterexample to \[1, Conjecture 1\]. In particular, for every_ \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), S<sub>2_n_+1</sub> _has_ 4_n_+2 _vertices,_ 2_n_+1 _hyperedges, and_ \(\epsilon(\mathcal{S}_{2n+1})=n\).<tbc>

<sup>1</sup>Lalou et al. \[1\] use \(\chi_p\) and \(\chi_p^2\). We write \(\chi_P\) and \(\chi_B\), respectively.

<tbc>_Proof._ We can color each _s<sub>i</sub>_ by _i_, and all _p<sub>i</sub>_ by _n_+1. This is a panchromatic coloring (Figure 1(a)), and \(\chi_P=n+1\). Any panchromatic (_n_+1)-coloring of S_<sub>n</sub>_ uses each color only once per hyperedge \(S\sqcup\{p_i\}\). The colors on _S_ have to be unique, thus \(\alpha=|S|=n\) and every _p<sub>i</sub>_ has the same color. Merging the unique colors gives \(n+1-\left\lceil\frac{n}{2}\right\rceil\) colors (Figure 1(b)). However, we can color each {_s<sub>i</sub>,p<sub>i</sub>_} distinctly (Figure 1(c)). Each hyperedge then contains _n_ colors, none of which is unique. Notice that \(\chi_B\le|V|/2=n\), thus \(\chi_B=n\) and \(\epsilon=\left\lceil\frac{n}{2}\right\rceil-1\).

Thus, the gap between \(\chi_B\) and the quantity in \[1, Conjecture 1\] is unbounded. In particular, adding any fixed constant to the right-hand side cannot make the conjecture valid in general.

Figure 1(a) shows a \(\chi_P\)-coloring of S_<sub>n</sub>_ attaining \(\alpha\). Figure 1(b) shows a bipanchromatic coloring obtained by merging unique colors. Figure 1(c) shows a bipanchromatic coloring with more colors.

For excess _n_, the three-hyperedge construction in \[5, Proposition 1\] uses at least 12_n_ vertices. The following construction uses 12_n_-6. It is obtained by enlarging S<sub>3</sub>. Replace each vertex by a group of 2_n_-1 vertices and each hyperedge by the union of the groups corresponding to its vertices.

**Proposition 2** (Three-hyperedge counterexamples)**.** _For_ \(n\in\mathbb{N}\)_, let S,P_<sub>1</sub>_,P_<sub>2</sub>_,P_<sub>3</sub> _be pairwise disjoint sets with_ |_S_|=6_n_-3 _and_ |_P<sub>i</sub>_|=2_n_-1_. Let_ \(V=S\sqcup P_1\sqcup P_2\sqcup P_3\), \(e_i=S\sqcup P_i\)_, and_ \(\Delta_n=(V,\{e_1,e_2,e_3\})\)_. The excess_ \(\epsilon(\Delta_n)\) _is equal to n._

_Proof._ Color the vertices of _S_ with distinct colors. Using |_P<sub>i</sub>_| additional distinct colors, color the vertices of each _P<sub>i</sub>_ with distinct colors. This is panchromatic, so \(\chi_P=|e_i|=8n-4\). Any \(\chi_P\)-coloring of \(\Delta_n\) uses each color only once per hyperedge \(S\sqcup P_i\), so only the colors on _S_ are unique, thus \(\alpha_{\chi_P}=|S|\). Now color the vertices of _S_ with distinct colors and repeat each such color on exactly one vertex in \(P_1\cup P_2\cup P_3\). This gives \(\chi_B=|S|\). Thus, \(\epsilon(\Delta_n)=(6n-3)-\left(8n-4-\left\lceil\frac{6n-3}{2}\right\rceil\right)=n\).

## 4 Bounds and minimality

Consider an arbitrary hypergraph _H_ with panchromatic number \(\chi_P\). For any integer \(k\le\chi_P\), let \(\beta_k=k-\left\lceil\frac{\alpha_k}{2}\right\rceil\). In particular, let \(\beta=\beta_{\chi_P}\). \[1, Conjecture 1\] asserts that \(\chi_B=\beta\), but this does not hold in general. However, for any _k_-panchromatic coloring of _H_ attaining \(\alpha_k\), the pairing argument used in \[1\] produces a bipanchromatic coloring with \(\beta_k\) colors. Thus, for every \(k\le\chi_P\) we obtain a lower bound for \(\chi_B\), and the largest of these bounds equals \(\chi_B\).

**Corollary 3** (Merging-based lower bound)**.** _For an arbitrary hypergraph H and for each integer_ \(k\le\chi_P\) _we obtain that_ \(\chi_B\ge\beta_k\)_. Furthermore, we have that_ \(\chi_B=\mathrm{max}_k\{\beta_k\}\).

**Lemma 4** (Equality cases and counterexample bounds)**.**

(i) _If_ \(\alpha\in\{0,1,2,\chi_P\}\)_, then_ \(\chi_B=\beta\)_. In particular, equality holds if_ \(\chi_P\le 3\).<tbc>

(ii) _If_ \(\chi_B\neq\beta\)_, then_ \(3\le\alpha\le\chi_P-1\) _and_ \(\left\lceil\chi_P/2\right\rceil\le\beta<\chi_B\le\chi_P-1\).

_Proof._ (i) Corollary 3 gives \(\chi_B\ge\beta\). If \(\alpha=0\), a \(\chi_P\)-coloring is already bipanchromatic, so \(\chi_B=\chi_P=\beta\). If \(\alpha>0\), no \(\chi_P\)-coloring is bipanchromatic, so \(\chi_B\le\chi_P-1\). For \(\alpha\in\{1,2\}\), \(\chi_B=\beta\). If \(\alpha=\chi_P\), then \(|V|=\chi_P\), so \(\chi_B\le\left\lfloor|V|/2\right\rfloor=\left\lfloor\chi_P/2\right\rfloor=\beta\), so \(\chi_B=\beta\).

(ii) By (i), \(3\le\alpha\le\chi_P-1\). Thus \(\beta\ge\chi_P-\left\lceil\frac{\chi_P-1}{2}\right\rceil=\left\lceil\frac{\chi_P}{2}\right\rceil\). Corollary 3 gives \(\beta<\chi_B\), and \(\alpha>0\) gives \(\chi_B\le\chi_P-1\) as above.

Let \(\rho=\chi_B/\beta\) denote the actual-to-conjectured ratio.

**Theorem 5** (Sharp ratio bounds)**.** _If_ \(|V|\ge 2\)_, then_ \(1\le\rho<2\)_, and the upper bound is asymptotically sharp. For_ \(\chi_P\ge 2\)_, the sharper bound_ \(\rho\le\frac{\chi_P-1}{\left\lceil\chi_P/2\right\rceil}\) _is attained for every fixed value of_ \(\chi_P\).

_Proof._ By Lemma 4 it holds that \(\rho\ge 1\), with equality precisely when (1) is true. Suppose that \(\chi_P\ge 2\). If \(\rho\neq 1\), then Lemma 4(ii) gives the upper bound. For \(n\ge 3\), Theorem 1 gives \(\rho(\mathcal{S}_n)=\frac{\chi_P-1}{\left\lceil\chi_P/2\right\rceil}\). The sharp bounds are strictly below 2 and tend to 2 as \(\chi_P\rightarrow\infty\).

_The order_ of a hypergraph _H_ is the number of its vertices |_V(H_)|. We show S<sub>2_n_+1</sub> has minimum order among hypergraphs satisfying \(\epsilon\ge n\).

**Theorem 6** (Excess-based minimum order)**.** _If a hypergraph H_=(_V,_E) _satisfies_ \(\epsilon(H)\ge n\)_, then_ \(|V|\ge|V(\mathcal{S}_{2n+1})|=4n+2\)_. Moreover, if_ \(\epsilon(H)=n\) _and_ |_V_|=4_n_+2_, then, after removing hyperedges that properly contain other hyperedges,_ \(H\cong\mathcal{S}_{2n+1}\).

_Proof._ By Lemma 4(ii), \(\beta\ge\left\lceil\chi_P/2\right\rceil\) and \(\chi_B\le\chi_P-1\). Hence

\(n\le\epsilon=\chi_B-\beta\le\chi_B-\left\lceil\chi_P/2\right\rceil\le\left\lfloor(\chi_B-1)/2\right\rfloor.\) (3)

Thus, \(\chi_B\ge 2n+1\), and consequently \(|V|\ge 2\chi_B\ge 4n+2=|V(\mathcal{S}_{2n+1})|\).

Suppose that \(\epsilon(H)=n\) and |_V_|=4_n_+2. It follows from (3) that \(\chi_B=2n+1\) and \(\beta=\left\lceil\chi_P/2\right\rceil=n+1\). Since \(\chi_P\neq\chi_B\) (\(\epsilon>0\)), we obtain \(\chi_P=2n+2\). Moreover, \(\left\lceil\frac{\alpha}{2}\right\rceil=\chi_P-\beta=n+1\). Since \(\alpha\neq\chi_P\) it follows that \(\alpha=2n+1\).

Consider a panchromatic \((\chi_P,\alpha)\)-coloring of _H_, and let _S_ be the set of its \(\alpha\) uniquely colored vertices. All remaining \(|V|-\alpha\) vertices have a common color _C_. For every vertex _v_ of color _C_, there is a hyperedge \(S\sqcup\{v\}\). Otherwise, if every hyperedge containing _v_ also contained another vertex of _v_’s color, recoloring _v_ with an existing unique color preserves panchromaticity and contradicts the supposed \(\alpha\). Removing hyperedges that properly contain other hyperedges leaves \(\mathcal{S}_{2\epsilon+1}\).

Every counterexample has at least three hyperedges. Choose a \(\chi_P\)-coloring attaining \(\alpha\). If every non-unique color occurred twice, then \(|V|=2\chi_P-\alpha\), so \(\chi_B\le\left\lfloor|V|/2\right\rfloor=\beta\), a contradiction. Thus some color _C_ occurs on at least three vertices. Since \(\alpha>0\), the same recoloring argument shows that each such vertex is the only _C_-colored vertex in some hyperedge. These hyperedges are distinct.

Proposition 2 attains this three-hyperedge minimum with \(\epsilon(\Delta_n)=n\) for every \(n\ge 1\). However, Theorem 6 implies that every hypergraph of minimum order satisfying \(\epsilon(H)\ge n\) has at least 2_n_+1 hyperedges. Thus, for \(n\ge 2\), the minimum numbers of vertices and hyperedges cannot be attained simultaneously.

## 5 Nondetermination By Corollary 3 and Lemma 4, if \(\chi_P>\alpha\ge 3\), then \(\chi_P-\lceil\alpha/2\rceil\le\chi_B<\chi_P\). We will show that every integer value of \(\chi_B\) in this range can be realized for the given pair \((\chi_P,\alpha)\). Thus, \(\chi_B\) cannot be expressed as a function of \(\chi_P\) and \(\alpha\) alone. **Proposition 7** (Realization of prescribed coloring parameters)**.** _Let p, a, b be integers satisfying_ \(3\le a0 and _e__n_+1, each of size _p_, whose intersection is a set _S_ of size _a_, as shown in Figure 2(a). Choose vertices \(x_0\in e_0\backslash S\) and \(x_{n+1}\in e_{n+1}\backslash S\), and write \(e_0=S\sqcup U\sqcup\{x_0\},e_{n+1}=S\sqcup W\sqcup\{x_{n+1}\},\) where |_U_|=|_W_|=_p-a_-1.
Since any hypergraph admitting a bipanchromatic _b_-coloring has at least 2_b_ vertices, we set \(n=max\{0,2b-(2p-a)\}\) (5) and add _n_ new vertices _x_1_,...,xn_. Let _X_={_x_0_,x_1_,...,xn,x__n_+1}. We then add _n_ new hyperedges \(e_i=\big(e_0\backslash\{x_0\}\big)\cup\{x_i\},\text{for all}i\in[n],\) see in Figure 2(b). This gives a _p_-uniform hypergraph _H_=(_V,_E), where \(V=S\sqcup U\sqcup W\sqcup X,\mathcal{E}=\{e_0,\dots,e_{n+1}\}.\) (6) By (4) and the definition of _n_, \(|V|\in\{2b,2b+1\}\). We define a _p_-panchromatic coloring of _H_ as follows: (1) The vertices of _S_ receive pairwise distinct colors. (2) The vertices of _U_ and _W_ are paired, with each pair receiving its own color. This introduces _p-a_-1 additional colors. (3) Introduce one new color. Assign that same color to every vertex of _X_. See Figure 2(b) for details. Every hyperedge contains all _p_ colors, so \(\chi_P=p\). Moreover, exactly the colors assigned to the vertices of _S_ are unique in any \((\chi_P,\alpha)\)-coloring, and hence \(\alpha=a\). To obtain a bipanchromatic _b_-coloring of _H_ (Figure 2(c)), we retain the colors assigned to the vertices of \(U\cup W\). Since \(|X|\le|S|\), we can pair the vertices of _X_ with a subset of _S_. We then merge the colors of the remaining vertices of _S_ in pairs, as indicated in the figure. We recolor any leftover vertex with an existing pair’s color. The resulting coloring is bipanchromatic and uses _b_ colors. Thus, \(\chi_B=b\). The construction realizes the prescribed parameters using at most \(\alpha\) hyperedges, each of size \(\chi_P\). Together with Lemma 4(i), this shows that \(\chi_P\) and \(\alpha\) uniquely determine \(\chi_B\) only when \(\alpha\in\{0,1,2,\chi_P\}\). The minimum number of vertices in a hypergraph _H_ with prescribed feasible parameters \((\chi_P,\alpha,\chi_B)\) is \(max\{2\chi_P-\alpha,2\chi_B\}\). Indeed, a \(\chi_P\)-coloring attaining \(\alpha\) gives \(|V|\ge\alpha+2(\chi_P-\alpha)=2\chi_P-\alpha\). A bipanchromatic \(\chi_B\)-coloring also gives \(|V|\ge 2\chi_B\).

For \(3\le\alpha<\chi_P\), the construction in Proposition 7 has exactly \(max\{2\chi_P-\alpha,2\chi_B\}\) vertices. In the remaining cases, Lemma 4(i) gives \(\chi_B=\beta\). Take two sets of size \(\chi_P\) intersecting in \(\alpha\) vertices, use them as hyperedges, and take their union as the vertex set. When \(\alpha=\chi_P\), this gives just one hyperedge. The panchromatic number is \(\chi_P\), and every maximum panchromatic coloring has unique colors precisely on the \(\alpha\) common vertices. The same lemma therefore gives bipanchromatic number \(\beta\). This construction has \(2\chi_P-\alpha=max\{2\chi_P-\alpha,2\beta\}\) vertices, attaining the lower bound.

## 6 Characterization of equality

Here we discuss conditions characterizing \(\chi_B=\beta\) (equivalently \(\epsilon=0\)) for an arbitrary hypergraph.

**Proposition 8** (Zero excess characterization)**.** _Assume that H is a hypergraph with_ \(\alpha\in\mathbb{N}\backslash\{1,2,4\}\)_. Then_ \(\chi_B=\beta\) _if and only if_ \(\beta=\left\lfloor\frac{|V|}{2}\right\rfloor\).

_Proof._ Assume that \(\chi_B=\beta\) and consider a \((\chi_P,\alpha)\)-coloring of _H_. Let _n_=3 if \(\alpha\) is odd and _n_=4 otherwise. If a color _C_ occurs at least _n_ times, recolor all vertices of color _C_ with _n_ existing unique colors, using each at least once. Merge the remaining \(\alpha-n\) uniquely colored vertices in pairs. This yields a \(\beta+1\) bipanchromatic coloring of _H_, contradicting \(\chi_B=\beta\). Therefore, if \(\alpha\) is odd, then every color occurs at most twice, and if \(\alpha\) is even, every color occurs at most thrice. If two distinct colors each occur three times, recolor their six vertices with six colors that are used only once (since \(\alpha\ge 6\)), and then merge the remaining uniquely colored vertices in pairs, again obtaining a coloring with \(\beta+1\) colors. Thus, at most one color occurs thrice, so \(|V|\in\{2\chi_P-\alpha,2\chi_P-\alpha+1\}\), and \(\lfloor|V|/2\rfloor=\beta\).

The converse follows from the definition.

For a hypergraph _H_ with \(\alpha=4\), the equality \(\chi_B=\beta\) requires further consideration. Consider mutually disjoint sets |_S_|=4, {_v,a,b,x_<sub>0</sub>_,x_<sub>1</sub>_,x_<sub>2</sub>} and |_P<sub>i</sub>_|=2 for _i_=1,2,3. We define two hypergraphs _H_<sub>-</sub> and _H_<sub>+</sub> whose hyperedge sets are, respectively

\(\mathcal{E}_-=\{S\sqcup P_i:i\in[3]\}\text{and}\mathcal{E}_+=\{S\sqcup\{v,x_0\},S\sqcup\{v,x_1\},S\sqcup\{v,x_2\},S\sqcup\{a,b\}\}.\)

Notice that |_V(H_<sub>-</sub>)|=|_V(H_<sub>+</sub>)|=10, \(\chi_P(H_-)=\chi_P(H_+)=6\), and \(\alpha(H_-)=\alpha(H_+)=4\). However, \(\beta=\chi_B(H_-)=4<|V|/2\) and \(\beta<\chi_B(H_+)=5=|V|/2\).

Therefore, if \(\alpha(H)=4\), we need an additional analysis. For a given hypergraph _H_=(_V,_E), define a simple graph _G<sub>H</sub>_=(_V,E_), where

\(E=\{uv:u,v\in V,\{u,v\}\cap e\neq\emptyset\text{for all}e\in\mathcal{E}\}.\)

**Proposition 9** (Matching reduction)**.** _Let H be a hypergraph with_ \(\alpha(H)=4\) _and let_ \(\nu\) _be the size of a maximum matching of G<sub>H</sub>. Then_ \(\chi_B=\beta\) _if and only if_ \(|V|+\nu\le 3\chi_P-4\).

_Proof._ Since \(\alpha=4\) and \(\beta=\chi_P-2\), then \(\chi_B\in\{\chi_P-2,\chi_P-1\}\). Consider any bipanchromatic _k_-coloring. Each color occurring exactly twice determines an edge of _G<sub>H</sub>_. These edges are vertex-disjoint, so they form a matching in _G<sub>H</sub>_. Therefore, we have at most \(\nu\) colors used exactly two times. Consequently, \(|V|\ge 2\nu+3(k-\nu)\), so \(k\le\chi_B\le\lfloor(|V|+\nu)/3\rfloor\).

If \(|V|+\nu\le 3\chi_P-4\), then \(\chi_B\le\chi_P-2=\beta\), and therefore \(\epsilon=0\).

For the converse, assume \(\epsilon=0\) and choose a panchromatic \(\chi_P\)-coloring attaining \(\alpha=4\).

If some color _C_ occurs at least four times, we can recolor all vertices of color _C_ with the four colors that are used only once. This produces a bipanchromatic coloring with \(\chi_P-1\) colors, contradicting \(\epsilon=0\).

Therefore, every color is used at most three times. Let C_<sub>k</sub>_ denote the number of colors used exactly _k_ times. Then, \(\chi_P=4+\mathcal{C}_2+\mathcal{C}_3\), and |_V_|=4+2C<sub>2</sub>+3C<sub>3</sub>.

The pairs corresponding to the C<sub>2</sub> color classes must form a maximum matching in _G<sub>H</sub>_\[_V_\\_S_\], where _S_ is the set of vertices receiving the four unique colors. Otherwise, an augmenting path would yield a larger matching, whose pairs could be assigned distinct colors in a panchromatic coloring of _H_ (the pairs intersect every hyperedge). The endpoints _u_ and _v_ of such an augmenting path belong to three-vertex color classes C<sub>3</sub>. Reassign the colors so that each matching pair forms its own color class. If _u_ and _v_ belong to the same three-vertex color class, assign the color of one of the four uniquely colored vertices to the third vertex of that class. This produces a \(\chi_P\)-coloring with three uniquely colored vertices, a contradiction. If _u_ and _v_ belong to different three-vertex color classes, assign the four unique colors to their other four vertices. This produces a bipanchromatic coloring with \(\chi_P-1\) colors, again a contradiction, since \(\chi_B=\beta=\chi_P-2\). Thus, \(\nu\le\mathcal{C}_2+4\), and thus \(|V|+\nu\le(4+2\mathcal{C}_2+3\mathcal{C}_3)+(\mathcal{C}_2+4)=3\chi_P-4\).

Given _H_ and promises \(\chi_P\) and \(\alpha\), \(\epsilon=0\) (or \(\chi_B=\beta\)) is decidable in polynomial time.

## 7 Order-aware improved bounds

In this section, we introduce another lower bound _L_ for the bipanchromatic number, based on our construction, and show that \(\beta\le L\le\chi_B\). Thus, _L_ improves the lower bound \(\beta\).

Consider a hypergraph _H_=(_V,_E) with \(|V|\ge 2\) and \(\alpha>0\). If \(\alpha\ge|V|/2\), then \(\chi_B=\lfloor|V|/2\rfloor\). Indeed, the unique vertices can be paired with the non-unique vertices, and any remaining vertices can be assigned colors so that every color used occurs at least twice. For the sunflower S_<sub>n</sub>_ (see Theorem 1), where \(n\ge 3\), we have \(\alpha=|V|/2\) and \(\chi_B=|V|/2\), while \(\chi_B/\beta\rightarrow 2\) as \(n\rightarrow\infty\).

We now consider the case \(0<\alpha<|V|/2\) and choose a panchromatic \(\chi_P\)-coloring of _H_ with \(\alpha\) unique colors. Let \(m=\chi_P-\alpha\) denote the number of colors used more than once. Suppose that color _i_ is used on _c<sub>i</sub>_ vertices, where

\(c_1\ge c_2\ge\cdots\ge c_m>1.\)

Observe that \(c_1+c_2+\cdots+c_m=|V|-\alpha\).

Let \(d\in[m]\) be the smallest index such that \(c_1+c_2+\cdots+c_d\ge\alpha\). Such an integer exists because \(|V|-\alpha>\alpha\).

Recolor all vertices in the first _d_ color classes with the \(\alpha\) unique colors so that each of these colors is used at least twice. This yields a bipanchromatic coloring of _H_ with \(L_d=\chi_P-d\) colors. Since \(c_i\ge 2\) for every _i_, we have \(d\le\lceil\alpha/2\rceil\). Consequently, \(\chi_B\ge L_d=\chi_P-d\ge\beta\). To obtain a bound for _d_, write Euclidean division of \(|V|-\alpha\) by \(m=\chi_P-\alpha\) as: \(|V|-\alpha=qm+r,\)
\(q=\left\lfloor\frac{|V|-\alpha}{\chi_P-\alpha}\right\rfloor\ge 2,0\le rDefine \(D=max\left\{\left\lceil\frac{\alpha}{q+1}\right\rceil,\left\lceil\frac{\alpha-r}{q}\right\rceil\right\},L=\chi_P-D.\) (7) Unlike _Ld_, which uses the chosen coloring, _L_ depends only on \(|V|,\chi_P\), and \(\alpha\). **Proposition 10** (Least class recoloring)**.** _Assume that the parameters of a hypergraph are defined as above. If_ \(0<\alpha<|V|/2\)_, then_ \(d\le D\le\left\lceil\frac{\alpha}{2}\right\rceil,\beta\le L\le L_d\le\chi_B.\) _Proof._ For every \(j\in[m]\), if \(c_j\ge q+1\), the first _j_ classes contain at least _j(q_+1) vertices. Otherwise, the last _m-j_ classes contain at most (_m-j)q_ vertices, so the first _j_ contain at least _jq+r_. Thus \(\sum_{i=1}^jc_i\ge jq+min\{j,r\}.\) The balanced sequence \(\widehat{c}_1=\cdots=\widehat{c}_r=q+1,\widehat{c}_{r+1}=\cdots=\widehat{c}_m=q\) attains equality for every _j_. Its first _j_ terms sum to at least \(\alpha\) exactly when both \(j(q+1)\ge\alpha\) and \(jq+r\ge\alpha\), so _D_ is its least such index. Therefore \(d\le D\). Since \(q\ge 2\) and \(r\ge 0\), the formula for _D_ gives \(D\le\lceil\alpha/2\rceil\), proving the stated bounds. _Remark._ If the three-hyperedge family described in \[5, Proposition 1\] satisfies \(0<\alpha<|V|/2\), then its parameters considered in Proposition 10 are _q_=3, _r_=0, and \(D=\alpha/3\). Thus \(L=\chi_P-\alpha/3=\chi_B\). The boundary case \(2\alpha=|V|\) is covered by the observation at the start of this section. So, our order-aware bound gives the exact bipanchromatic number throughout that family. Let \(U=min\{\chi_P-1,\lfloor|V|/2\rfloor\}\). If \(0<\alpha<|V|/2\), then \(\beta\le L\le L_d\le\chi_B\le U\), and _U_ is an upper bound for \(\chi_B\). Now, we examine the relations between _U_, \(\chi_B\), and _L_. **Theorem 11** (Improved bound ratio)**.** _The bounds L and U always satisfy_ \(5U\le 6L+1,1\le\frac{\chi_B}{L}\le\frac{U}{L}\le\frac{5}{4}.\) (8) _In particular,_ \(L\le 3\) _implies U=L. For all feasible inputs,_ \(\frac{\chi_B}{L}\le\frac{6}{5}+\frac{1}{5L}.\) (9)

_Proof._ Use the balanced sequence \(\widehat{c}_1,\dots,\widehat{c}_m\) from Proposition 10. These are not necessarily the actual color-class sizes of _H_. Their sum is \(|V|-\alpha\), and _D_ is the least index for which the first _D_ terms sum to at least \(\alpha\).

Set \(g=U-L\ge 0\). We prove that \(L\ge 5g-1\). Since \(U\le\chi_P-1=L+D-1\), we obtain \(g\le D-1\). By minimality of _D_, it follows that<tbc>

\(\widehat{c}_D(D-1)\le\widehat{c}_1+\cdots+\widehat{c}_{D-1}\le\alpha-1.\)

<tbc>Consequently,

\(\alpha\ge\widehat{c}_Dg+1.\) (10)

Since \(\sum_{i=1}^m\widehat{c}_i=|V|-\alpha\), and \(\widehat{c}_i\le\widehat{c}_D\) for \(i\ge D\),

\(|V|=\alpha+\sum_{i=1}^{D-1}\widehat{c}_i+\sum_{i=D}^m\widehat{c}_i\le\alpha+(\alpha-1)+\widehat{c}_D(m-D+1).\) (11)

Since \(U=L+g=\alpha+m-D+g\) and \(U\le|V|/2\) (by definition), inequality (11) yields

\((\widehat{c}_D-2)(m-D+1)\ge 2g-1.\) (12)

We use \(L=\alpha+m-D\) and \(m-D\ge 0\) to consider the following four cases:

\(\begin{array}{ c c c c }
\widehat{c}_D & \text{From(12)} & \text{From(10)} & \text{Conclusion} \\
2 & g=0 & - & L\ge 5g-1 \\
3 & m-D\ge 2g-2 & \alpha\ge 3g+1 & L\ge 5g-1 \\
4 & m-D\ge g-1 & \alpha\ge 4g+1 & L\ge 5g \\
\ge 5 & - & \alpha\ge 5g+1 & L\ge 5g+1
\end{array}\)

Therefore, \(5g\le L+1\), which gives \(5U\le 6L+1\).

For \(L\le 3\) we obtain _U=L_. For \(L\ge 4\),

\(\frac{U}{L}\le\frac{6}{5}+\frac{1}{5L}\le\frac{5}{4}.\)

_Remark._ The conclusions of Theorem 11 also hold with _L<sub>d</sub>_ in place of _L_. Indeed, \(L\le L_d\le\chi_B\), so \(5U\le 6L+1\le 6L_d+1\) and \(\chi_B/L_d\le\chi_B/L\le 5/4\).

We prove that for fixed parameters \((|V|,\chi_P,\alpha)\), without more information, the bound _L_ is the best possible.

**Proposition 12** (Optimality)**.** _For any valid parameters_ \((|V|,\chi_P,\alpha)\)_, with_ \(0<\alpha<\frac{|V|}{2}\) _, there exists a hypergraph with these prescribed parameters that satisfies_ \(\chi_B=L\).

_Proof._ Compute _q_ and _r_ as before. Set \(m=\chi_P-\alpha\) and consider pairwise disjoint sets _S,P_<sub>1</sub>_,...,P<sub>q</sub>,Z_ with \(|S|=\alpha\), |_P<sub>i</sub>_|=_m_, and |_Z_|=_r_. Choose \(R\subseteq P_1\) with |_R_|=_r_. We define the hypergraph _H_=(_V,_E), where<tbc>

\(V=S\sqcup\sqcup_{i=1}^qP_i\sqcup Z,\mathcal{E}=\{S\sqcup P_i:i\in[q]\}\cup\{S\sqcup(P_1\backslash R)\sqcup Z\}.\)

<tbc>Thus \(|V|=\alpha+qm+r\) is attained, and every hyperedge has size \(\chi_P\). Now, we define a coloring of _H_ such that \(\alpha\) vertices in _S_ receive distinct colors, each _P<sub>i</sub>_ uses all _m_ remaining colors<tbc>

<tbc>once, and, if _r\>_0, each color from _R_ is used exactly once on _Z_. This gives a panchromatic coloring of _H_ with \(\chi_P\) colors. In any panchromatic \(\chi_P\)-coloring of _H_, precisely the vertices in _S_ have unique colors, so \(\alpha\) is attained.

Now, we consider a bipanchromatic _k_-coloring of _H_. Assume that precisely \(s\le\alpha\) colors occur on _S_. Each of the other _k-s_ colors occurs in every _P<sub>i</sub>_, so at least _q_ times. Those also absent from _P_<sub>1</sub>\\_R_ must occur on _Z_, so they occur at least _q_+1 times. At most _m-r_ of the _k-s_ colors occur on _P_<sub>1</sub>\\_R_. Therefore<tbc>

\(|V|\ge 2s+q(k-s),|V|\ge 2s+(q+1)(k-s)-(m-r).\)

<tbc>Substituting \(s\le\alpha\), \(|V|=\alpha+qm+r\), and \(\chi_P=\alpha+m\) gives<tbc>

\(q(\chi_P-k)\ge\alpha-r,(q+1)(\chi_P-k)\ge\alpha.\)

<tbc>By the definition of _D_, it follows that

\(\chi_P-k\ge max\left\{\left\lceil\frac{\alpha}{q+1}\right\rceil,\left\lceil\frac{\alpha-r}{q}\right\rceil\right\}=D.\)

Thus every bipanchromatic coloring has at most \(\chi_P-D=L\) colors. Since also \(L\le\chi_B\) by Proposition 10, we obtain \(\chi_B=L\).

Therefore, at every feasible triple in this range, any universally valid lower bound using only \((|V|,\chi_P,\alpha)\) is at most _L_. Since _L_ is itself valid, it is the strongest such lower bound.

**Corollary 13** (Optimal ratio guarantees)**.** _For L, the factor_ 5/4 _in_ (8) _is attained. The constant_ 6/5 _in_ (9) _is asymptotically sharp as_ \(L\rightarrow\infty\)_. These are optimal constants from_ \(|V|,\chi_P,\alpha\).

_Proof._ For any \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), Proposition 7 describes a hypergraph whose parameters \((|V|,\chi_P,\alpha,\chi_B)\) are (12_n_-2,6_n,_3_n_+1,6_n_-1). Here we obtain _q_=3, _r_=0, _D=n_+1, and _L_=5_n_-1, so

\(\frac{\chi_B}{L}=\frac{6n-1}{5n-1}=\frac{6}{5}+\frac{1}{5(5n-1)}.\)

This is 5/4 at _n_=1 and tends to 6/5 as \(n\rightarrow\infty\). Proposition 12 confirms optimality.
